title: DeepSeek put the architecture for their always-on autonomous agent on GitHub
content:
Research prototype for reference only, not an official DeepSeek product. This code grew out of our team's day-to-day development work, with much of the engineering done by coding agents. Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Review and adapt it before using it in your own environment.
We have adapted it for publication, so it is not identical to our internal version or the implementation described in Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System. Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype.
dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.
It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. docs/000-philosophy.md explains the principle and what it asks of the operator.
Setup has many steps, so an agent does it with you. Ask your coding agent:
Read SETUP.md in this repository and set up dsh-superagent with me.
It asks one short question at a time, shows the full plan once, and then installs and configures everything. SETUP.md is what it follows.
Read the numbered documents in order; each builds only on the ones before it.
- 000 Philosophy
- 001 Domain model
- 002 Authorization
- 003 Execution
- 004 Prompts
- 005 Panel
- 006 Deployment: manual setup, configuration, upgrades and troubleshooting
- 007 Architecture
- 008 Cookbook: adding a Source
pnpm check runs the typecheck, the tests and the build.

report.summary: DeepSeek published a research prototype of an always-on coding agent that watches a GitHub repo, executes requested work in isolated sessions, and replies with pull requests.
report.background: Coding agents have shifted in two years from autocomplete to autonomous task execution — Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Devin, OpenHands and Aider all now take a goal and produce patches. The bottleneck is no longer model capability but scaffolding: authorization, session isolation, event triggering, and human handoff. DeepSeek previously outlined this in a design paper, 'Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System,' and has now released a reference implementation under its deepseek-ai GitHub org. Two details are notable: the code was substantially written by coding agents themselves, and the product surface is Feishu (Lark) alongside GitHub, reflecting DeepSeek's Chinese enterprise context. The release fits a broader industry move away from chat windows toward always-on, event-driven agents that sit inside existing team workflows rather than being invoked manually.
key_points: What it actually does: dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent scoped to a single GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub events and optionally Feishu. When an authorized person asks for work, it opens a work item, executes it in its own agent session and directory, and answers back in the original conversation — typically by opening a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a human.

The core design principle is attention budgeting: 'take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible.' Since an agent acting for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, it acts only when asked or when a team-written rule permits it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use the result. The philosophy is documented in docs/000-philosophy.md.

DeepSeek is explicit that this is research code, not a product: it may contain bugs, its style and engineering practices may be inconsistent, and it differs from both the internal version and the published design paper — some paper designs are future directions, not implemented here. Scoping is deliberately narrow: one repository.

The repo is documentation-first. Eight numbered documents build sequentially — philosophy, domain model, authorization, execution, prompts, panel, deployment, architecture, plus a cookbook for adding new event 'Sources.' Setup itself is designed to be done by a coding agent reading SETUP.md, asking one question at a time, showing the full plan, then installing. pnpm check runs typecheck, tests and build.

A meta-signal: much of the engineering was done by coding agents. DeepSeek is both shipping an agent framework and demonstrating the agent-builds-agent loop, with humans reviewing and adapting the output before it reaches production.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes the competitive frontier: the differentiator is shifting from raw model capability to permissioning, isolation and attention management — the scaffolding that decides when an agent may act and when it should stay silent. A public reference architecture lowers the bar for any team wanting an internal always-on agent. For developers, it is a forkable template for repo-level automation (issue triage, review response, PR generation), but it is research-grade, so security review and adaptation are mandatory, and the single-repo scope is a realistic constraint rather than a limitation to hack around. The agent-assisted setup pattern is itself worth copying. For regular users, the effect is indirect: repository bots that respond to plain requests will spread, with clearer human-in-the-loop checkpoints — and the honest framing that an agent's scarcest resource is human attention.
report.tools: Start with the dsh-superagent-prototype repo and its SETUP.md, and follow the numbered docs to understand the authorization and execution model. DeepSeek Harness is the runtime it bundles into. For comparison, study OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI as alternative agent scaffolds; LangGraph or AutoGen if you want to build the orchestration yourself; GitHub Apps and webhooks for trigger plumbing; and the Feishu/Lark open platform if you need chat-side triggers.
